title: Reading old paintings: symbols, perspective and anachronism
description: Paintings made before 1900 were meant to be read. A sleeping dog means fidelity, a lamp that has just gone out means time is up, and a vanishing point tells you where the painter wanted you to stand. Each question shows a real painting or a detail from one and asks what it told the people who first saw it: hidden skulls, saints' attributes, moral jokes, impossible bouquets and Bible stories set in the painter's own street.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: This painting is called *Landscape with the Fall of Icarus*. Where is Icarus?
questions.description: In the myth, Icarus flew too close to the sun on wings of feathers and wax. The wax melted and he fell into the sea. Search the whole scene before you answer.

images.alt: A wide coastal landscape: in the foreground a ploughman in a red shirt guides a horse along curving furrows, a shepherd with his flock stands behind him, a large sailing ship rides the bay at right, and a low sun sits on the horizon.
images.caption: After Pieter Bruegel the Elder, *Landscape with the Fall of Icarus*, probably 1560s. Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Landscape_with_the_Fall_of_Icarus_-_Brussels,_Royal_Museums_of_Fine_Arts_of_Belgium_-_Google_Arts_%26_Culture.jpg).

images.alt: Close-up of the lower right corner: two bare legs kick up out of the green water, with small white feathers scattered on the waves nearby.
images.caption: Detail: Icarus goes under, legs first.

options.text: Only his legs show, kicking in the water just below the big ship at lower right
He is still falling, a tiny figure silhouetted against the setting sun
He is the ploughman in the red shirt, shown after he survived the fall
He lies washed up on the rocky island in the middle of the bay

questions.explanation:
Just below the big ship at lower right, a pair of pale legs splashes into the sea, with a few loose feathers drifting down. That is all you see of the painting's title subject.

Everyone else carries on with their day. The ploughman watches his furrow, the shepherd gazes up at the wrong part of the sky, and the angler on the bank minds his line. In Ovid's telling these three look up in astonishment. Here nobody notices. A Flemish proverb says the farmer kept ploughing, meaning that ordinary work goes on while someone dies, and W. H. Auden's poem *Musée des Beaux-Arts* reads the painting the same way.

Check the sun as well. It is already half-set on the horizon, nowhere near where Icarus fell. Technical studies suggest this canvas is an early copy of a lost Bruegel original, but the museum still treats the composition as his.

questions.title: A long pale smear floats above the floor between the two men in Holbein's *The Ambassadors*. What is it?
questions.description: The panel is a life-size double portrait of two French envoys in London. This detail shows the bottom center.

images.alt: A long, pale, diagonal shape streaks across a patterned marble floor between the dark shoes of two standing men. Seen face-on it is hard to read.
images.caption: Hans Holbein the Younger, *The Ambassadors*, 1533 (detail). National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hans_Holbein_the_Younger_-_The_Ambassadors_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg).

images.alt: The same detail rotated and compressed along its long axis: the smear becomes a human skull seen from the side, with eye socket, cheekbone and teeth.
images.caption: The detail rotated about 24 degrees and squeezed to a quarter of its length, roughly what your eye does when you look along the panel from the side.

images.alt: The whole painting: two richly dressed men stand either side of a two-shelf table crowded with globes, scientific instruments, a lute and books, with the pale diagonal shape on the floor between them.
images.caption: The whole panel. A small crucifix peeks out from behind the curtain at top left. Hans Holbein the Younger, *The Ambassadors*, 1533. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hans_Holbein_the_Younger_-_The_Ambassadors_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg).

options.text: A skull, stretched so that it only takes shape when you look at the panel from a sharp angle
A fallen fur stole, painted loosely to contrast with the sharp detail above it
Old damage that a restorer covered with a neutral patch of paint
The shadow of a sword held by someone standing outside the picture

questions.explanation:
It is a human skull, painted with a trick called anamorphosis. Holbein stretched it along a diagonal, so face-on it looks like a smear. Stand close to the wall and look along the panel from high on the right, or low on the left, and the distortion cancels out. A skull appears. The second image imitates that view by rotating the detail and squeezing it along its long axis.

The skull is a *memento mori*, a reminder of death, placed among fine furs, globes and scientific instruments that show off the two men's wealth and learning. It is also a puzzle, and a boast about Holbein's skill. One theory says the painting hung beside a door or a stair, so a visitor walking past would catch the skull at the right angle. Another says you were meant to view it through a glass tube. Neither has been proved.

The restoration answer isn't entirely wrong. Parts of the skull had flaked away and were rebuilt in 1997, but the shape itself is Holbein's. He added one more religious sign: a small crucifix, half-hidden behind the green curtain at top left, often read as a hint of hope beside the reminder of death.

questions.title: Which of these can you find in or around the convex mirror on the back wall of the Arnolfini Portrait?
questions.description: Jan van Eyck painted this couple in a room in Bruges in 1434. The detail enlarges the mirror, which takes up only a small part of the panel.

images.alt: A man in a dark fur-trimmed cloak and wide black hat holds the hand of a woman in a full green gown in a bedroom. A brass chandelier hangs above them, a small round mirror hangs on the back wall, and a small shaggy dog stands at their feet.
images.caption: Jan van Eyck, *The Arnolfini Portrait*, 1434. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Van_Eyck_-_Arnolfini_Portrait.jpg).

images.alt: Close-up of the round convex mirror in a spiked frame set with ten tiny painted roundels. Its curved glass reflects the room in miniature. Ornate script is painted on the wall above it, and a string of amber prayer beads hangs to the left.
images.caption: Jan van Eyck, *The Arnolfini Portrait*, 1434 (detail). National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Van_Eyck_-_Arnolfini_Portrait.jpg).

options.text: The couple, seen from behind
Two more figures standing in the doorway, facing the couple
Tiny scenes from the Passion of Christ set into the frame
A Latin inscription above it: *Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434*, 'Jan van Eyck was here 1434'
The painter at his easel, brush raised
A priest reading the marriage vows

questions.explanation:
The mirror shows the room from the other side: the backs of the couple and, in the doorway facing them, two tiny visitors, one in blue and one in red. The figure in red is often taken to be van Eyck himself. Unlike Velázquez in *Las Meninas*, he isn't shown painting. There is no priest anywhere in the room. The ten roundels in the frame hold scenes from the Passion, Christ's suffering and death.

Above the mirror, van Eyck lettered his signature in large script on the wall, the way proverbs were written on walls at the time: 'Jan van Eyck was here, 1434.' In 1934 Erwin Panofsky argued that the two visitors and this eyewitness signature make the painting a record of a wedding with witnesses. Many historians now doubt that. They read it instead as a betrothal, a legal arrangement between husband and wife, or a memorial to a wife who had already died.

The mirror itself is too good to be real. Nobody in 1434 could make a convex mirror this large.

questions.title: Many first-time viewers assume the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait is pregnant. What do art historians usually conclude?

images.alt: Detail of the woman: a white linen headdress and a green gown with long fur-lined sleeves and a trailing skirt. One hand rests on the front of the skirt, which is gathered up and bulges forward below a high belt.
images.caption: Notice how much cloth is gathered up under her hand. Jan van Eyck, *The Arnolfini Portrait*, 1434 (detail). National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Van_Eyck_-_Arnolfini_Portrait.jpg).

options.text: Probably not: she is holding up the heavy folds of a very full, fashionable gown
Clearly pregnant: the painting was commissioned to announce an heir
Pregnant, which is why a bed is in the room: it is a birthing chamber
Wearing a padded costume for a religious play

questions.explanation:
The rounded shape comes from the dress. Fashionable gowns of the 1430s had a high waist and a huge skirt, and a woman gathered the front up to walk. Van Eyck and his contemporaries painted virgin saints with exactly the same swelling silhouette. The cloth itself was a boast: the more fabric you wore, the richer you looked, and Arnolfini was a merchant in the cloth trade.

Neither woman proposed as the sitter is known to have had children. The bed isn't evidence either, because wealthy households used beds in reception rooms as seating.

The question isn't completely closed. One recent theory reads the painting as a memorial to a wife who had died, possibly in childbirth. Others read her gesture as a hope for children rather than a sign that she is expecting.

questions.title: In Steenwyck's still life, which objects stand for death and passing time, and not for the pleasures that death cuts short?
questions.description: Harmen Steenwyck painted this in Leiden around 1640. His buyers knew how to read every object on the table.

images.alt: A table-top still life lit by a diagonal shaft of light: a skull lying on its side, a brass oil lamp with a wisp of smoke, a lute, a recorder and a long wind instrument, stacked books, a sword in a black sheath, a small round case, a stoneware jug and a large spiral shell.
images.caption: Harmen Steenwyck, *Still Life: An Allegory of the Vanities of Human Life*, about 1640. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Harmen_Steenwijck_-_Vanitas_Still-Life_-_WGA21768.jpg).

options.text: The skull
The brass oil lamp, just blown out and still smoking
The small round watch case lying beside the sword
The lute, the recorder and the shawm
The books
The Japanese sword in its lacquered sheath

questions.explanation:
This is a *vanitas*, named after Ecclesiastes: 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.' The objects fall into two groups.

The first group shows what people spend their lives on. The books stand for learning. The lute, recorder and shawm, along with the wine flask, stand for pleasure. The costly Japanese sword stands for wealth and power.

The second group says that all of it ends. The skull sits in the shaft of light. The lamp has just gone out, with a thread of smoke still rising, and the watch keeps ticking.

The tropical shell does double duty. It was an expensive collector's piece, and, like the skull, an empty home whose occupant had died. Many Dutch still lifes can be read the same way: list the pleasures, then find the reminder.
questions.references: [National Gallery: An Allegory of the Vanities of Human Life](https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/harmen-steenwyck-still-life-an-allegory-of-the-vanities-of-human-life) · [Wikipedia: Vanitas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanitas)

questions.title: In the Dutch paintings Chardin learned from, a soap bubble was a stock symbol. What did it usually stand for?
questions.description: Jean Siméon Chardin painted several versions of this scene in the 1730s.

images.alt: A young man leans out of a stone window opening and blows through a straw, swelling a large, clear bubble. A small child peeks over the ledge beside him, and a glass of soapy water stands on the sill.
images.caption: Jean Siméon Chardin, *Soap Bubbles*, probably 1733–34. National Gallery of Art, Washington. Public domain (CC0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jean_Sim%C3%A9on_Chardin,_Soap_Bubbles,_probably_1733-1734,_NGA_994.jpg).

options.text: The shortness and fragility of human life
Cleanliness and good housekeeping
Idle wealth, because soap was an expensive import
The new science of light, following Newton's work on colors in thin films

questions.explanation:
The Latin saying *homo bulla*, 'man is a bubble', goes back to the Roman writer Varro, and Erasmus made it popular. A bubble floats, shines for a moment and bursts. That made it a favorite prop in vanitas still lifes, and children blow bubbles in many seventeenth-century Dutch paintings. Chardin knew that tradition well.

Whether he meant the full sermon is less certain. Some writers think he simply liked painting a quiet moment of play, and the painting never spells out a moral. Still, a viewer in the 1730s would have recognized the old symbol: a young man leaning over a sill, blowing a bubble that is about to pop.

questions.title: Which of these help explain why Simone Martini set this Annunciation against solid gold instead of a sky or a room?
questions.description: Painted in 1333 for the cathedral of Siena.

images.alt: A wide gilded altarpiece with pointed Gothic arches. At the center an angel kneels, holding an olive branch, before a woman in dark blue who shrinks back on her throne, with a vase of lilies between them. A standing saint fills each side panel, and everything sits against flat gold.
images.caption: Simone Martini and Lippo Memmi, *Annunciation with Saint Margaret and Saint Ansanus*, 1333. Uffizi, Florence. Public domain (CC0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Simone_Martini_%E2%80%94_Annunciation_with_St._Margaret_and_St._Ansanus.jpg).

options.text: Gold stood for heavenly light, lifting the scene out of ordinary space and time
In a candlelit church, the gold leaf flickered and glowed as the flames moved
Gold leaf was costly, so it honored the holy figures and showed what the patrons had spent
Painters of the time had not yet learned how to paint a convincing sky

questions.explanation:
The gold was a choice. Some thirty years earlier, Giotto had painted deep blue skies across the Arena Chapel in Padua, and Simone could paint a sky too.

Gold did things a sky couldn't. It set Gabriel and Mary in a timeless, heavenly space. In a dim cathedral lit by candles, the burnished leaf caught every flame and seemed to give off light of its own. It also displayed money and devotion. Patrons went on writing gold into contracts long after painters had mastered landscape: in 1445, the confraternity that commissioned Piero della Francesca's Misericordia altarpiece still required a gilded background.

Look at the greeting that runs from the angel's mouth toward Mary: *Ave gratia plena dominus tecum*, 'Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.' The letters are raised and gilded, part of the gold surface itself.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Gold ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_ground) · [Wikipedia: Annunciation with Saint Margaret and Saint Ansanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annunciation_with_Saint_Margaret_and_Saint_Ansanus)

questions.title: Why are the kneeling people in Piero della Francesca's *Madonna of Mercy* so much smaller than the Virgin who shelters them?

images.alt: Against a gold background, a very tall Virgin in a red dress spreads her dark blue cloak wide with both arms. Eight much smaller men and women kneel in prayer beneath it, one of them wearing a black hood with eyeholes.
images.caption: Piero della Francesca, *Madonna of Mercy*, central panel of the Misericordia Polyptych, 1445–62. Museo Civico, Sansepolcro. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Piero_della_Francesca_-_Polyptych_of_the_Misericordia_-_Madonna_of_Mercy_-_WGA17449.jpg).

options.text: Size shows importance: the holiest figure is painted largest, whatever the distance
They kneel further back in space, so perspective makes them smaller
They are children from an orphanage the confraternity ran
Piero ran out of room on the panel and squeezed them in

questions.explanation:
This is hierarchical scale: size shows rank, not distance. The kneeling figures are members of the confraternity that commissioned the altarpiece, one of them wearing the hood members wore in processions. They are as close to us as Mary is, and her cloak curves around them like the apse of a church.

Piero was one of the great theorists of perspective and gave every figure a solid, three-dimensional body. Here he still followed the older rule, and the Virgin's importance sets her size. Compare Masaccio's *Trinity* in Florence, painted a generation earlier. There the donors kneel at the same scale as the saints, which was new at the time.

questions.title: Why does the Christ Child in Berlinghiero's thirteenth-century *Madonna and Child* look like a small, serious adult?

images.alt: A gold-ground panel: the Virgin in a dark blue mantle holds on her arm a child in an orange robe whose face, proportions and expression look like those of a grown man.
images.caption: Berlinghiero, *Madonna and Child*, 1230s. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Public domain (CC0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Madonna_and_Child_MET_DT5279.jpg).

options.text: On purpose: he was shown as the all-wise Word of God in a small body, not as an ordinary baby
Medieval painters rarely saw infants, who were kept out of sight
Tight swaddling was believed to make babies mature faster, so painters showed them older
Later restorers repainted the face in an adult style

questions.explanation:
Art historians usually explain it through theology. Christ was believed to be fully God from birth, complete in wisdom, so painters gave him a grown man's proportions and face, like a small adult seated on his mother's arm. The formula came from Byzantine icons, and Berlinghiero, working in Lucca, followed it closely: the gold ground, Mary's hand gesturing toward her son, the flat patterned drapery.

These painters weren't trying to paint a real baby. Babies began to look like babies in fifteenth-century Italy, as painters studied real bodies and filled pictures with chubby infants and cherubs.

questions.title: Why is the Virgin's mantle so often an intense blue, as in Sassoferrato's *Virgin in Prayer*?

images.alt: Half-length figure of a young woman with bowed head and hands pressed together in prayer, a white veil over her hair, wrapped in a deep, brilliant blue mantle against a plain dark background.
images.caption: Sassoferrato, *The Virgin in Prayer*, 1640–50. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sassoferrato_-_Jungfrun_i_b%C3%B6n.jpg).

options.text: The finest blue, ultramarine, was made from lapis lazuli and could cost as much as gold, so using it honored her
Blue was the cheapest pigment, which suited a humble woman
The Gospels describe Mary wearing a blue cloak
Blue had no special meaning; it was chosen to balance the red and white

questions.explanation:
The blue is ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli, a stone mined in north-eastern Afghanistan and brought to Europe, probably through Venice. Turning the stone into pigment took long grinding, sifting and washing, and the best ultramarine could be worth as much as gold. Painters' contracts sometimes specified the grade of blue to be used for the Virgin.

Giving her the most precious color was an act of devotion, and over time the blue also came to stand for her purity and status. The Gospels never describe her clothes.

Sassoferrato, painting around 1640–50, made the most of it. Against the plain dark background, the ultramarine blazes. It stayed expensive until a synthetic version arrived in the 1820s.

questions.title: In Leonardo's *Last Supper*, the ceiling beams and the tops of the wall hangings all recede toward one point. Where is it?

images.alt: A long wall painting: thirteen men sit along one side of a table covered with a white cloth, in a room with a coffered ceiling, dark hangings receding along both side walls, and three bright windows in the back wall. An arched doorway cuts into the bottom center of the painting.
images.caption: Leonardo da Vinci, *The Last Supper*, about 1495–98. Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Leonardo_da_Vinci_-_The_Last_Supper_high_res.jpg).

images.alt: The same painting with yellow lines drawn along the tops of the hangings on both side walls and along two ceiling beams. All four lines meet in a dot on Christ's head.
images.caption: Four receding edges, extended until they meet.

options.text: At Christ's head, in the center of the picture
At the window behind the apostles on the far right
At Judas's hand as it reaches for the bread
Below the table, at the arched doorway

questions.explanation:
The receding lines of the room, from the coffered ceiling beams to the tops of the hangings on both walls, converge on Christ's head, near his right temple. Wherever your eye enters the picture, the lines lead it there. The bright window behind him frames his head like a halo, without any gold.

There is a small hole in the plaster at that point. It probably held a nail, and Leonardo stretched strings from it to mark out the perspective lines on the wall.

The arched gap at the bottom isn't part of the design. Someone cut a doorway through the wall in 1652, and it destroyed Christ's feet.

questions.title: Masaccio painted this chapel onto a flat church wall around 1425–28. Where did he place the vanishing point, and what did that do for a visitor?

images.alt: A tall fresco of a painted classical chapel. Fluted pilasters and a round arch frame a coffered barrel vault. Inside, Christ hangs on the cross with God the Father standing behind him and Mary and John on either side. Two donors, in red and in dark blue, kneel in profile outside the arch.
images.caption: Masaccio, *Holy Trinity*, about 1425–28. Santa Maria Novella, Florence. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Masaccio,_Holy_Trinity,_1425-28,_Santa_Maria_Novella,_Florence.jpg).

options.text: Low, at about the eye level of an adult standing in the church, so the vault seems to open upward into a real chapel beyond the wall
High, at God the Father's head, so visitors had to kneel to see the scene correctly
At the center of the cross, so the scene looks the same from anywhere in the church
Far to one side, toward the church door, so the illusion only worked as you walked in

questions.explanation:
Masaccio set the horizon low, on the ledge between the two kneeling donors, roughly where an adult standing in front of the wall would be looking. From there the coffered vault recedes upward and back, and you look up into it as you would into a real side chapel. Vasari wrote that it seems as if there is a hole in the wall.

The donors kneel outside the painted arch, as if in the church beside you, and they are the same size as the holy figures, which was new in the 1420s.

Below them, cropped out of this photo, a painted tomb holds a skeleton with a warning: 'I was once what you are, and what I am you will also be.' The fresco climbs from that reminder of death, past the donors, up to God.

questions.title: Which saint did Raphael paint here?
questions.description: Saints are identified by their attributes, objects taken from their stories. This one leans on hers.

images.alt: A young woman in a blue dress with green sleeves and a crimson mantle looks up at the sky with one hand on her chest. Her other arm rests on a large wooden wheel, and a calm river landscape stretches behind her.
images.caption: Raphael, *Saint Catherine of Alexandria*, about 1507. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Raffael_020.jpg).

options.text: Catherine of Alexandria, with the spiked wheel on which she was to be tortured
Mary Magdalene, with the wheel of fortune she turned her back on
Barbara, with the mill wheel of the tower where her father imprisoned her
Agnes, with a cartwheel from the procession of her martyrdom

questions.explanation:
The wheel identifies her. According to legend, Catherine was a fourth-century princess of Alexandria who refused to give up her faith. The emperor Maxentius ordered her broken on a spiked wheel, but a thunderbolt shattered it before it could harm her, and she was beheaded instead.

Painters often add a sword and a martyr's palm. Raphael left those out and showed her looking up toward a golden break in the clouds, hand on heart. The wheel alone was enough for a viewer around 1507, just as keys meant Peter and a lamb meant Agnes. Her wheel also gave its name to a spinning firework, the Catherine wheel.

The other options borrow real saints but not their attributes: Mary Magdalene carries a jar of ointment and Barbara a tower.
questions.references: [National Gallery: Saint Catherine of Alexandria](https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/raphael-saint-catherine-of-alexandria) · [Wikipedia: Catherine of Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_of_Alexandria)

questions.title: Francesco del Cossa's saint holds up a slender stem with something odd at its tip. What is it, and why?

images.alt: A woman against a gold ground holds a palm frond in one hand. In the other she delicately raises a thin stalk topped by a small, curious two-part bloom.
images.caption: Francesco del Cossa, *Saint Lucy*, about 1473–74. National Gallery of Art, Washington. Public domain (CC0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Francesco_del_Cossa,_Saint_Lucy,_c._1473-1474,_NGA_369.jpg).

images.alt: Close-up of her hand: the thin stalk forks into two curling shoots, each ending in a realistic human eye.
images.caption: Francesco del Cossa, *Saint Lucy*, about 1473–74 (detail). National Gallery of Art, Washington. Public domain (CC0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Francesco_del_Cossa,_Saint_Lucy,_c._1473-1474,_NGA_369.jpg).

options.text: A pair of human eyes, because Lucy is the protector of sight and legend says her eyes were torn out
Poppy seed heads, a symbol of the sleep of death
Two pearls, a sign of her noble birth
Olive buds, for peace between the church and the empire

questions.explanation:
Two human eyes sprout from the stem like a flower. She is Saint Lucy of Syracuse, martyred in 304. Her name, Lucia, shares a root with Latin *lux*, light, and devotion to her as a protector of sight probably gave her this emblem.

Stories from the fifteenth century on say her eyes were gouged out or that she removed them herself. Painters usually put the eyes on a dish, and del Cossa turned them into a strange, elegant bloom. The palm in her other hand is the standard sign of a martyr. She is still the patron saint of the blind.

questions.title: Which details in Antonello da Messina's painting identify the scholar at the desk as Saint Jerome?

images.alt: A scholar in red robes reads at a wooden desk on a raised platform inside a vast vaulted hall, seen through a stone arch. A peacock and a partridge stand on the front ledge, and a shadowy animal walks along the colonnade at right.
images.caption: Antonello da Messina, *Saint Jerome in his Study*, about 1475. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Antonello_da_Messina_-_St_Jerome_in_his_study_-_National_Gallery_London.jpg).

options.text: The lion padding through the shadows of the hall at right
His red cardinal's robes
The peacock on the front ledge
The partridge on the front ledge

questions.explanation:
Jerome, the fourth-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin, has two standard attributes.

The first is a lion. Legend says he pulled a thorn from a lion's paw in the desert and it stayed with him. Here it walks down the aisle at right.

The second is a cardinal's red robes, often with a wide red hat. That is itself an anachronism: there were no cardinals in Jerome's day, but later centuries gave him the rank as an honor.

The birds on the ledge carry meanings of their own but could appear with anyone. The peacock stood for immortality, because its flesh was thought never to decay. The partridge stood for truth, because it was believed to recognize its mother's call.

questions.title: Which of these pairings of object and meaning fit Crivelli's *Annunciation*?
questions.description: Painted in 1486 for a friary church in Ascoli Piceno, in central Italy.

images.alt: A tall panel of a sunlit Renaissance street in steep perspective. At left an angel holding a white lily kneels beside a bishop who carries a model of a town. At right, through an open wall, a young woman kneels at a lectern. A thin golden beam slants from a glowing opening in the sky into her room, a peacock perches on the balcony above, and an apple and a cucumber lie on the front ledge.
images.caption: Carlo Crivelli, *The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius*, 1486. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Annunciation,_with_Saint_Emidius_-_Carlo_Crivelli_-_National_Gallery.jpg).

images.alt: Detail of the front ledge: a green cucumber and a red-and-yellow apple lying on pale stone above a lettered inscription.
images.caption: Carlo Crivelli, *The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius*, 1486 (detail). National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Annunciation,_with_Saint_Emidius_-_Carlo_Crivelli_-_National_Gallery.jpg).

options.text: The apple on the ledge: the forbidden fruit of the Fall
The cucumber beside it: the promise of resurrection
The peacock on the balcony: immortality
The lily Gabriel carries: Mary's purity
The golden beam from the sky: the Easter sunrise
The dove traveling down the beam: peace between Ascoli and the pope

questions.explanation:
Crivelli packs the scene with signs. The apple and the cucumber on the front ledge form a pair. The apple recalls the fall of Adam and Eve. The cucumber, or gourd, stands for resurrection and redemption, the undoing of that fall through the child Mary is about to conceive. The peacock meant immortality, because people believed its flesh never decayed. Gabriel's white lily marks Mary's purity.

The golden beam is the moment of conception itself. It shoots from a burst of light in the sky, passes through a neat opening in the wall and reaches Mary, carrying the dove of the Holy Spirit. So the dove isn't a political emblem, even though the painting does carry a civic message about Ascoli.
questions.references: [National Gallery: The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius](https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/carlo-crivelli-the-annunciation-with-saint-emidius) · [Wikipedia: The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Annunciation,_with_Saint_Emidius)

questions.title: Why has Crivelli moved the Annunciation to a busy fifteenth-century Italian street, with a local bishop showing Gabriel a model of a town?
questions.description: The bishop is Saint Emidius, patron saint of Ascoli Piceno, the town the altarpiece was made for. Along the bottom of the panel runs the inscription LIBERTAS ECCLESIASTICA.

images.alt: Detail: a winged angel in gold brocade kneels in the street holding a lily, while a bishop in a mitre beside him holds out a detailed model of a walled town with towers.
images.caption: Saint Emidius interrupts Gabriel to show him the town. Carlo Crivelli, *The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius*, 1486 (detail). National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Annunciation,_with_Saint_Emidius_-_Carlo_Crivelli_-_National_Gallery.jpg).

options.text: Ascoli won a measure of self-government from the pope in 1482, and the news arrived on 25 March, the feast of the Annunciation, so the painting celebrates both
Nobody in Italy knew what Nazareth looked like, so painters had no alternative
The friars claimed the Annunciation had really taken place in Ascoli
Church rules of the time required every altarpiece to include the local patron saint

questions.explanation:
Ascoli was ruled by the pope. In 1482 Pope Sixtus IV granted it a degree of self-government, and the news reached the town on 25 March, the feast of the Annunciation. From then on, the feast was celebrated with a great procession to the friary this altarpiece was made for.

Crivelli ties the sacred story to the civic one. Emidius holds a model of Ascoli, whose towers can still be recognized. The coats of arms along the base belong to the pope, the town and its bishop. LIBERTAS ECCLESIASTICA, 'church liberty', was the title of the papal document granting Ascoli its rights. On the bridge behind, a man reads a message that has just arrived by carrier pigeon. It may be the news of that document, and it echoes Gabriel's own delivery.

Painters routinely set Bible stories in their own streets and clothes. Here the local setting is the point.

questions.title: A small dog sleeps curled at the feet of Titian's *Venus of Urbino*. What did such a dog usually signify in Renaissance painting?

images.alt: A nude woman reclines on white sheets, holding a small posy of roses and looking directly at the viewer. A small dog sleeps curled at her feet, and behind her two maids kneel at a large chest in a palace room.
images.caption: Titian, *Venus of Urbino*, 1538. Uffizi, Florence. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tiziano_-_Venere_di_Urbino_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg).

images.alt: Manet's version: a nude woman reclines on a white bed in the same pose, looking straight out. A maid brings her a large bouquet, and at her feet a black cat stands with its back arched.
images.caption: Manet's answer, 330 years later. Édouard Manet, *Olympia*, 1863. Musée d'Orsay, Paris. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Edouard_Manet_-_Olympia_-_Google_Art_Project_3.jpg).

options.text: Fidelity, especially within marriage
The pleasures of the hunt and of country life
The approach of death, since dogs guided souls to the underworld
Nothing in particular: Titian painted his own pet into many pictures

questions.explanation:
A dog, and especially a small, sleeping lapdog, was a common sign of fidelity. The Latin *fido* means 'I trust'. That is one reason some historians read this 1538 painting as a celebration of marriage. In the background two maids search a *cassone*, the kind of chest that held a bride's clothes. Others think the woman is a courtesan, and the debate isn't settled.

The dog's meaning is clearest in what Manet did with it. His *Olympia* of 1863 borrows Titian's composition, but where the sleeping dog was, a black cat stands with its back arched. Visitors to the 1865 Paris Salon took the swap, together with her name and her direct gaze, as signs that she was a prostitute, and the painting caused a scandal.

questions.title: Why could this bouquet by Ambrosius Bosschaert never have stood on a real table?
questions.description: Painted in 1621. Look at which flowers share the vase.

images.alt: A dense bouquet in a round glass vase on a stone ledge: striped tulips, a yellow iris, roses, a peony and many smaller flowers, every bloom fully open, with a butterfly and a fallen cyclamen on the ledge and a painted inscription below.
images.caption: Ambrosius Bosschaert the Elder, *Bouquet of Flowers in a Glass Vase*, 1621. National Gallery of Art, Washington. Public domain (CC0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ambrosius_Bosschaert,_Bouquet_of_Flowers_in_a_Glass_Vase,_1621,_NGA_94743.jpg).

options.text: The flowers bloom at different times of year; the painter combined studies made over many months
Tulips had not yet reached the Netherlands in 1621
Glass vases like this one could not be made until the nineteenth century
Several of the flowers are invented species that never existed

questions.explanation:
Early Dutch flower pieces are collages. Bosschaert painted individual blooms from life as each came into flower, spring tulips and irises, early-summer roses and so on, then combined the studies into one ideal bouquet with every flower at its peak and none drooping. No single week of the year could have supplied this vase.

The tulips were real enough. They had been grown in Dutch gardens since the 1590s, and striped ones were among the most prized flowers of the day, years before the tulip mania of 1636–37.

A viewer in 1621 would have admired the impossible abundance and the skill. Many would also have seen a quieter theme: the butterfly and the fallen cyclamen on the ledge are reminders that all this beauty will fade.

questions.title: In Vermeer's *The Love Letter*, a seascape with a sailing ship hangs on the wall behind the two women. What does it add?

images.alt: View through a dark doorway into a bright room: a seated woman in a yellow satin jacket, holding a stringed instrument, looks up at a standing maid who has just handed her a letter. Two paintings hang behind them, a landscape and a seascape with a sailing ship, and a pair of slippers and a broom lie in the foreground.
images.caption: Johannes Vermeer, *The Love Letter*, about 1669–70. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Johannes_Vermeer_-_%27De_liefdesbrief%27_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg).

options.text: A comment on the letter: love was often compared to a voyage at sea, so the painting hints at how the affair is going
A record of the family business, since the absent husband was a ship's captain
Nothing in particular: Dutch walls were simply crowded with paintings
News of a death at sea, which the letter is bringing

questions.explanation:
Dutch viewers were used to pictures within pictures that comment on the main scene. Love as a sea voyage was a familiar image in emblem books and poems: the lover as a ship at the mercy of the weather, with calm water for a happy affair and storms for trouble. This sea looks rough, which suggests a stormy romance.

Vermeer adds other clues. The woman holds a cittern, and music-making was a standard sign of love. Her slippers lie kicked off in the foreground and the broom leans forgotten, so the housework has been abandoned. The landscape above the seascape shows a traveler on a sandy road, which may point to the absent man who wrote the letter.

questions.title: Which details in Jan Steen's *Beware of Luxury* warn about where this household is heading?
questions.description: Painted in 1663. A slate propped in the corner reads *In weelde siet toe*, roughly 'In good times, beware'. In Dutch, 'a Jan Steen household' still means a chaotic home.

images.alt: A crowded, chaotic room: a young woman in yellow satin holds a glass of wine next to a grinning man, an older woman sleeps at the table, and children raid a cupboard and play with a pipe and a string of pearls. A dog eats from a dish on the table, a monkey sits by a clock on the wall, a basket hangs from the ceiling, and a pig noses at a sprig of roses in the corner among scattered cards.
images.caption: Jan Steen, *Beware of Luxury*, 1663. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jan_Steen_-_Beware_of_Luxury_%28%E2%80%9CIn_Weelde_Siet_Toe%E2%80%9D%29_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg).

options.text: The basket hanging overhead, holding a crutch, a sword and a leper's clapper
The monkey playing with the clock
The pig nosing at a rose
The dog on the table eating the pie
The sleeping housewife, resting after a day of honest work
The cupboard, well stocked and neatly kept, a sign that order will return

questions.explanation:
Steen built the picture as a joke with a sermon inside. The punishment hangs overhead: a basket holding a crutch, a sword and a clapper, the rattle a leper used to warn people away. Poverty, violence and disease are waiting to fall. The monkey fiddling with the clock recalls the saying that time is forgotten in folly. The pig nosing a rose acts out 'roses before swine', something precious wasted. The dog helps itself to the pie while nobody watches.

The two wrong answers describe the opposite of what you see. The lady of the house has dozed off, probably from drink, and the household is running wild. Her children are raiding the cupboard for glassware, and one of them is smoking a pipe. The man in front, modeled by Steen himself, laughs off a woman scolding him while cards and food litter the floor.

questions.title: Hogarth's *The Tête à Tête* shows a young aristocratic couple shortly after their wedding. Which details show the marriage is already failing?

images.alt: An elegant, untidy drawing room: at right a young man in a hat slumps in a chair with his legs stretched out and a small dog beside him, at center a young woman stretches her arms beside a tea table, and at left an older man in black walks away holding papers with one hand raised. An overturned chair and an open music book lie on the carpet.
images.caption: William Hogarth, *Marriage A-la-Mode: 2, The Tête à Tête*, about 1743. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Marriage_A-la-Mode_2,_The_T%C3%AAte_%C3%A0_T%C3%AAte_-_William_Hogarth.jpg).

images.alt: Detail of the slumped husband: a small grey dog sniffs at his coat pocket, and a sword lies on the carpet near his feet.
images.caption: William Hogarth, *Marriage A-la-Mode: 2, The Tête à Tête*, about 1743 (detail). National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Marriage_A-la-Mode_2,_The_T%C3%AAte_%C3%A0_T%C3%AAte_-_William_Hogarth.jpg).

options.text: A small dog is pulling a woman's lace cap out of the husband's pocket
A broken sword lies at his feet
The steward is walking away with a stack of unpaid bills
The husband has just come home from a long day managing the family estate
The couple is sharing a quiet breakfast, attentive to each other

questions.explanation:
This is the second scene of *Marriage A-la-Mode*, Hogarth's six-picture story of an arranged marriage, painted around 1743 and sold to a wide public as engravings. It is the morning after a long night for both of them.

The husband slumps in his chair, still in his hat, and his dog sniffs at a lace cap poking out of his pocket. It isn't his wife's. The broken sword by his feet suggests a brawl. The wife stretches after her own night: the overturned chair and the music on the floor point to a party at home. At the left, the steward raises a hand in despair and walks off with a fistful of bills.

The couple aren't looking at each other at all. Hogarth meant his series to be read like a novel, one telling detail at a time.
questions.references: [National Gallery: Marriage A-la-Mode: 2, The Tête à Tête](https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/william-hogarth-marriage-a-la-mode-2-the-tete-a-tete) · [Wikipedia: Marriage A-la-Mode (Hogarth)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_A-la-Mode_(Hogarth))

questions.title: There is a bare, unfinished patch on Mrs Andrews's lap. What was supposed to go there?

images.alt: A young man with a gun under his arm and a dog at his feet stands beside a young woman in a pale blue dress seated on a bench under an oak. To the right stretches a wide view of fields, wheatsheaves, pastures and a distant church under a cloudy sky.
images.caption: Thomas Gainsborough, *Mr and Mrs Andrews*, about 1750. National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Mr_and_Mrs_Andrews.jpg).

images.alt: Close-up of the woman's lap: her hands rest on a patch of flat brownish paint with no clear object in it, surrounded by the finished folds of her blue silk skirt.
images.caption: Thomas Gainsborough, *Mr and Mrs Andrews*, about 1750 (detail). National Gallery, London. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Mr_and_Mrs_Andrews.jpg).

options.text: Nobody knows for sure; a baby, a book, a fan or a bird shot by her husband have all been suggested
A pet cat, painted out after the animal died
Nothing: the patch is damage from a twentieth-century cleaning
A basket of eggs, the traditional attribute of a new bride

questions.explanation:
The canvas simply isn't finished there. Gainsborough left the area in her lap unpainted, and nobody knows why. The National Gallery suggests it may have been kept for a baby to be added later. Other guesses include a book, a fan, or a game bird shot by her husband, who stands with his gun and dog.

The rest of the picture is easier to read. It has been called a triple portrait, of Robert Andrews, his wife and his land. Most of the fields in view belonged to him. The neat wheatsheaves and well-stocked pastures show off a well-run estate, displayed as proudly as the couple themselves.
questions.references: [National Gallery: Mr and Mrs Andrews](https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/thomas-gainsborough-mr-and-mrs-andrews) · [Wikipedia: Mr and Mrs Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr_and_Mrs_Andrews)

questions.title: Which of these statements about Rembrandt's *Night Watch* are true?

images.alt: A huge group portrait: armed militiamen with muskets, pikes and a banner surge forward from a dark archway. At the center a captain in black with a red sash strides beside a lieutenant in pale yellow, and a small girl in a golden dress glows among the men at left.
images.caption: Rembrandt, *The Night Watch*, 1642. Amsterdam Museum, on loan to the Rijksmuseum. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Nightwatch_by_Rembrandt_-_Rijksmuseum.jpg).

options.text: It shows a daytime scene: darkened varnish made it look like night, and the nickname stuck
It was cut down on all four sides in 1715 to fit a wall in Amsterdam's town hall
The militiamen shown in it paid for it themselves
The glowing girl with a dead chicken at her belt is a walking emblem of the company
Rembrandt painted it by torchlight to record a real night patrol
The company rejected it and never hung it

questions.explanation:
Its real title is *Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq*, and the company is setting out in daylight. For most of its history the canvas was coated in varnish that darkened with age, which is how it came to be called the Night Watch. The varnish came off in the 1940s, but the name stayed.

The captain and members of his company paid Rembrandt about 1,600 guilders to be included. The painting hung in their hall until 1715. It was then moved to the town hall and trimmed on all four sides to fit between columns, losing figures at the left.

The small girl lit up in gold carries the company's symbol. The claws of the dead chicken at her belt refer to the *clauweniers*, the arquebusiers.
